wormald.shelfmark: London, British Library, Harley MS 55, ff. 1–4 (Part A)
wormald.liebermann_date: c. 1040 (medical texts); f. 3b II–III Eg c. 1050; f. 5 I–II Cn c. 1120
wormald.wormald_date: s. xi¹ (Ker's date for the medical hand, which must also hold for the code and memorandum because both are glossed in the Wulfstan hand, p. 186; Table 4.1, p. 164); scribal doodles added s. xi (p. 187); titles to both codes in a hand of 's. xvi ex' (p. 185)
wormald.wormald_origin: Worcester (Table 4.1, p. 164); York or Worcester: the property memorandum points to York, but three glosses by the Worcester 'tremulous hand' show it at Worcester by the thirteenth century (p. 188). Certainly from an episcopal library and marked by the Wulfstan hand (p. 188). The leaves once ended a larger MS—either a school-MS (suggested by the medical tract and the doodles) or a Gospel-book (suggested by the memorandum) (pp. 186–8). Joined to Part B probably only c. 1600; given by John Selden to Simonds D'Ewes (letter of 1649); Selden may have joined, even excised, the two parts (pp. 185–6 and n. 98).
wormald.laws: II Eg, III Eg (the two-part code 'II–III Edgar'), with distinctive readings shared with other Wulfstan MSS: inserted clauses on plough-alms, soul-scot and church-peace; London added beside Winchester as standard for weights and measures; penalty for underweight wool; a clause on Friday fasts (II Eg 5:1, '7 ælces Frigedæges') found only here (substantive changes listed p. 189 n. 111: II Eg 2:3, 5:1–3, III Eg 8:1–3)
wormald.laws_liebermann: II Eg, III Eg, I Cn, II Cn
wormald.other_contents: Four half-sheets with three items: a medical tract on 'half-dead disease' (hemiplegia), five pages from f. 1r; II–III Eg (two pages and a line); after a two-line gap, Archbishop Oswald's memorandum of lands lost by the church of York (S 1453; Robertson LIV), glossed and given a title and an imprecation in the Wulfstan hand (pp. 186, 188). Eleventh-century scribal doodles between code and memorandum ('Ælfmer Pattafox ...') (p. 187).
wormald.overview: The first four leaves of Harley 55 are an early eleventh-century fragment, once the end of a larger MS, holding a medical tract, a copy of II–III Edgar and Archbishop Oswald's list of estates lost by York. The code and the memorandum carry corrections and additions in the hand Ker identified as Archbishop Wulfstan's, so this is the earliest of the law-books to show Wulfstan's own intervention; its text of Edgar shares several substantive additions with other Wulfstan manuscripts and alone has a clause on Friday fasting. It was at York or Worcester (certainly at Worcester in the thirteenth century), and there is no clear sign of its association with the mid-twelfth-century Cnut quire (Part B) until the later sixteenth century; Selden may have joined them.
wormald.liebermann_superseded: Liebermann dated the medical text c. 1040 and II–III Edgar c. 1050, and gave one siglum A to the whole of Harley 55; Wormald, since the code and Oswald’s memorandum are glossed in Wulfstan’s hand, dates all three items s. xi¹ and treats Part A as a separate MS from the Cnut quire, joined to it probably only c. 1600 (pp. 185–6, 188, 253).
wormald.key_quote: 'Harley's leaves were marked in one or other library by the ‘Wulfstan hand’' (p. 188)
wormald.doubts: GUIDE: Liebermann's dates c. 1040 / c. 1050 for Part A are superseded (s. xi¹, checked in image of Table 4.1 and p. 186). GUIDE: guide calls the Oswald item ‘a charter’; Wormald describes it as a memorandum/plaint of lands taken from York (S 1453). GUIDE: guide says Part B was ‘bound in by the binder’; Wormald finds no sign of association before titles were added in a hand of ‘s xvi ex’ and a 1649 letter, and suggests Selden joined (perhaps even excised) the two parts (pp. 185–6, 253–4). Liebermann's single siglum A covers both parts (p. 185 n. 96); Wormald separates Harley 55(A) and 55(B); Ker nos. 225–6. In the II–III Eg readings Wormald aligns A with D and G² (Wulfstan MSS) against G and Quadripartitus (p. 189; ‘G²’ checked in image). Early-modern ‘L’ marks and marginal numbers probably Joscelyn's; enlarged initials possibly Wulfstan's or a close associate's (p. 189 and n. 113). The folio range ff. 1–4 is inferred from ‘the first four folios’ (p. 185) and the facsimile reference ff. 3v–4v (p. 188 n. 107). Lambarde did not know this Edgar text; its special readings leave no trace in Archaionomia (pp. 185, 253). Part A’s Edgar and Part B’s Cnut were transcribed into CCCC 383 at different times (p. 185 n. 97; p. 230 n. 266). The ‘scepige’ error at III Eg 7 recurs in Harley 55(B) at II Cn 25 (p. 255 n. 351).
verify_notes: overview: removed unsupported ‘only copy of II–III Edgar in this form’; Part B described as mid-twelfth-century (p. 185: a century and a half later; p. 253) and the c. 1600 union stated with Wormald’s caution.
liebermann_superseded: removed the drafter’s inference about Wulfstan’s death date; added the single-siglum point (p. 185 n. 96, p. 253).
pages: removed duplicate Table entry and ‘outside this range’ note; added 178, 186 nn. 99–100.

wormald.wormald_heading: 7 Law as pamphlet? BL, Harley MS 55(B)
wormald.liebermann_date: c. 1040 (medical texts); f. 3b II–III Eg c. 1050; f. 5 I–II Cn c. 1120
wormald.wormald_origin: No assigned provenance ('???' in Table 4.1); a link with houses still producing vernacular MSS, such as Worcester or Rochester, is possible but unsupported (p. 255). Transcribed by Nowell and so used by Lambarde; the Parker circle took from it the missing part of I Cn for Corpus 383 and entered some chapter numbers; probably not bound with part A before Selden's time; 16th-century titles and law-only ink foliation ('3'–'11') (pp. 253–4; 185–6; 230 n. 266).
wormald.laws: I–II Cn only (the twelfth-century 'vulgate' text, with an extra prologue claiming Cnut's rule of Norway, shared with Consiliatio Cnuti)
wormald.laws_liebermann: II Eg, III Eg, I Cn, II Cn
wormald.other_contents: A self-contained quire (last, probably blank, leaf cut away); two columns on thick, yellowish parchment; red opening clause and initials; text largely continuous; well-thumbed. Nothing but Cnut's code.
wormald.overview: A self-contained quire of the mid-twelfth century holding nothing but Cnut's code in Old English, written in two columns on rough parchment: of all the surviving manuscripts it looks most like a working law-book. It could have circulated on its own as a pamphlet, and was probably joined to the older Edgar leaves of Harley 55(A) only in early modern times, perhaps by Selden. Its text is a plain and reasonably careful copy, and its very existence shows that Old English law was not yet of purely antiquarian interest a lifetime after the Conquest, though nothing is known of where it was made.
wormald.liebermann_superseded: Liebermann gave the whole of Harley 55 one siglum (A) and dated its Cnut text c. 1120; Wormald, following Ker, dates the Cnut quire s. xii^med and treats it as a separate booklet probably not joined to part A before Selden's time (pp. 185–6 and n. 96; 253–4 and n. 341).
wormald.key_quote: the manuscript which behaves most like a book of law might be expected to behave ends by posing the biggest mystery of all. (p. 253)
wormald.doubts: Ker, Catalogue no. 226. Wormald's siglum in Table 4.1 is [A], the same as Liebermann's for the whole of Harley 55. GUIDE: guide's one entry (MsA) merges Harley 55(A) and 55(B); date for Cnut (c. 1120) should be s. xii^med. The guide's note already says Cnut was originally a separate manuscript. Liebermann's reading ealswa at II Cn 84:4 is wrong: 'ealra' visible under UV (p. 255 n. 352). Folio range ff. 5–13 inferred from 'first four folios' + 'the nine that follow' (p. 185); Wormald cites f. 13r/v (p. 255 nn. 351–2). Joscelyn glossed Nero A.i's Cnut usually from Lambarde's edition, itself based on Harley 55(B) (p. 186 n. 97; p. 254 n. 343). Titles in a hand of 's xvi ex' (p. 185).

overview: 'joined only in the 16th or 17th century' softened to 'probably' (p. 186: 'perhaps Selden'); 'still being made for use' replaced by Wormald's actual inference (p. 255).
liebermann_superseded: kept but recast; Liebermann had already dated Cnut separately (c. 1120), so the point is the date and the booklet's separateness.
